content.body:
My father took MiraLAX every morning for twelve years. He died at 64 of complications from chronic constipation.

Three months ago I sat in the same exam-room chair he sat in and my doctor reached for the same prescription.

I almost said yes — until my husband asked one question that would have saved my father's life.

I'm 44.

My father has been gone for nine years now. The spring our youngest started kindergarten.

The death certificate said "complications from chronic constipation, sepsis pathway." I didn't even understand what that meant until I read the discharge summary on the plane home from the funeral.

He was a quiet man. A bridge engineer for the state DOT for thirty-six years. He measured things for a living.

The MiraLAX showed up on his kitchen counter the year I turned 30.

His GP said the line I've thought about every week since.

"This is your new best friend now."

That exact phrase.

My father wrote it down on a Post-it inside the kitchen cabinet. I found it cleaning out the house. New best friend. In his engineer's handwriting.

For twelve years he scooped the white powder into his orange juice every morning at 6:15 AM. I watched him do it from my teenage kitchen, and then later from the kitchen I came home to visit.

He'd say "I'm regular as a clock."

He'd say it like a small joke at family dinners. Like a man reporting from a bridge inspection.

I believed him.

The year before he died, he started saying his belly felt "tight." He was 63. The GP said keep up the MiraLAX, maybe try a little Metamucil with it.

He did.

The week he died I didn't know how bad it had gotten. The hospital said sepsis. The hospital said impaction. The hospital used the word "perforation" and I asked them to please not use the word "perforation" with my mother in the room.

Twelve years of managed output.

He died of the thing they were managing.

I started slipping around the time my fortieth birthday came and went.

Every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth.

By 42 it was every four to five days at best.

The bloat showed up at 8 PM like a guest who would not leave. I stopped wearing my wrap dress because I look six months pregnant by dinner. Stopped tucking shirts in. Started pulling sweaters around my waist in every photo.

I dread thinking about when I will poop.

I stopped saying that out loud somewhere around my 40th birthday because I could hear my mother saying it about my father.

The strain hour at 6 AM, the door locked, my knees pulled up to my chest, my eyes closed for ninety minutes while the rest of the house slept.

Pebble stools when I did go. Rabbit pellets. Blood on the paper one morning — I cried in the bathroom and then I went to work.

The drawer.

I stood in front of it one night and I made myself list it out loud.

MiraLAX. White powder, the orange juice in the morning.

Metamucil. Three orange tubs stacked in the back.

Magnesium citrate. The green-and-yellow soda bottle I'd chug on Sunday nights. Tastes like grapefruit lighter fluid.

Magnesium glycinate. The calmer one. Didn't really move anything.

Senna. The brown tablets. The whip I'd take when I had a flight Tuesday.

Dulcolax suppositories. The box in the back. The emergency drawer.

Milk of Magnesia. Four months of chalky nightly chugs. Bloated belly that wouldn't quit. Stopped working after three rounds.

Castor oil. Three days. The smell. Three hours of cramping for ten minutes of release. Never again.

Probiotics. We fell for Align. Thirty a month for six months. Three good weeks. Then nothing.

Smooth Move tea. The kettle on at 9 PM every Sunday.

Prune juice. Every morning until I gagged at the sight of the bottle.

Triphala. Two weeks of working, then nothing.

Fiber gummies. Two different brands. Made the bloat worse.

The squatty potty under the bathroom sink.

The colonoscopy at 41. Nothing remarkable.

A pelvic-floor PT referral I canceled twice and never went to.

I closed the drawer.

Stood there in the dark.

Half of those were in my father's cabinet too. I'd been buying them my whole life and not seeing it.

This past New Year's I drove down to help my mother sort my father's old papers.

We sat at the same kitchen table I grew up at.

In the back of the cabinet behind the coffee mugs, I found an unopened MiraLAX packet.

I held it.

Sat down with it in my hand.

Set it on the counter next to my coffee.

Drove home that night.

Booked the first available appointment with my new GP — my old one had retired the year before — and made a note in my phone to actually go this time.

Three weeks later I was sitting in Exam Room 4 of the same medical-park complex my father had used for fifteen years.

I didn't realize that until I walked in and saw the framed lithograph of a covered bridge on the wall.

Same lithograph my father used to make fun of. A bridge engineer making fun of a bridge lithograph for fifteen years.

The chair.

The vinyl exam chair with the cracked armrest.

The same chair.

I sat down in it and I could feel my father sitting in it.

My husband came with me because I had been crying in the car for two weeks. He sat in the side chair with his hands on his knees.

The doctor was kind. He was thorough. He listened for six minutes.

Then he said "you've tried a lot."

Pulled out the prescription pad.

"Let's start you on a daily MiraLAX. It'll be your new best friend."

The exact phrase.

Twelve years late.

I almost said yes. My hand was already reaching for the script.

My husband leaned forward in the side chair.

Quiet. Not aggressive. The way he asks the auto mechanic things.

"Before she fills it — can someone look at what's actually broken? Her dad was on this for twelve years."

The doctor paused.

Said he could refer me to a functional-medicine specialist if I wanted. Didn't push. Pulled a card out of his desk drawer and handed it to me.

Dr. Aurelia Marchetti. Foundation Functional Medicine. Cottage office on Maple Street.

I took the card.

Walked out without the prescription.

Sat in the parking lot for forty minutes before I could start the car.

I almost canceled the appointment with Dr. Aurelia twice.

Two hundred dollars for an intake form that asks me about my father felt like grief tourism.

I drove there anyway.

A converted craftsman cottage at the end of Maple Street. Wood floors. A window seat with a wool throw on it. The smell of bergamot tea coming out of what used to be a dining room.

The receptionist offered me a cup. I drank it.

Dr. Aurelia came out herself to call my name. Not a medical assistant. Mid-fifties, gray bob, reading glasses on a beaded chain.

She booked one patient per hour. I was the one patient.

The intake form was six pages. One whole page about my father.

She didn't talk about treatment that first visit. She said: "Before we change anything, I want to see what's actually there."

Ordered a microbiome stool panel.

Three hundred and forty dollars out of pocket.

I almost didn't send it in.

I sent it in.

Ten days later the results came back and we booked a follow-up.

Second appointment.

She turned her monitor toward me. Pulled up the chart. Color-coded bars across a screen that looked like a soundboard.

"Your bowel frequency — every four to five days — is the surface. The damage underneath is ten years worse than that number suggests."

She let that sit.

Then she said the thing I wrote down in my phone notes app in the parking lot afterward.

"The laxative is like repainting a house with a crumbling foundation. The walls look fine from the street. The beams are rotting underneath."

She paused.

"Your father's beams rotted for twelve years while his doctor was repainting."

I started crying in the chair. She handed me a tissue from a wooden box and waited.

Then she walked me through the panel.

She pointed to the first bar.

"Bifidobacterium. These should be in the top three populations in a healthy colon. Yours is in the bottom ten percent. These are the bacteria that ferment fiber into the chemical signals that tell your colon to contract."

Second bar.

"Akkermansia muciniphila. Should be at three to five percent. Yours is at zero point four. These bacteria maintain the mucus layer that protects the wall of your gut. When they're gone, the wall thins. Constipation accelerates the loss, because stool sits there longer and dries the mucus out."

She looked up from the screen.

"Every day on MiraLAX is a day the Akkermansia don't come back."

Third bar.

"Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Should be five to ten percent. Yours is at zero point eight. These produce butyrate. Butyrate is the single most important short-chain fatty acid for the health of your colon wall and the signal that tells the muscles to contract."

She turned the screen back toward herself.

"Short-chain fatty acids — acetate, butyrate, propionate — are the chemical signals your bacteria send to the muscles of your colon. Without those signals, the muscles sit in their chairs. They are not broken. They are not getting the message."

I said, "But my GP said more fiber —"

She cut in. Gently.

"Fiber is the raw material. If the bacteria that ferment it aren't there, more fiber is more concrete you can't pour because there's no mixer. Eighty percent of people with what you have don't respond to more fiber. That's published. That's not me being clever."

I started to say something about probiotics and she got there first.

"Most probiotics send one violinist to an empty stage. They show up in your gut, play for a week, and pass through. The category you actually need is fermentation. Pre-finished postbiotics. Delivered daily. The way traditional cultures got them from kombucha, kefir, fermented vegetables, every day, without thinking about it."

She tapped the screen.

"That is what your father never got. Your grandmother probably did, every day, without knowing why."

Then she said the thing about MiraLAX.

"MiraLAX is polyethylene glycol. It pulls water into the colon. That's all it does. It doesn't feed the bacteria. It doesn't restore the signal. It manages output. It doesn't heal anything."

She looked at me for a long moment.

"It is repainting. Twelve years of repainting is what we saw on your father's death certificate."

I sat in the chair and looked at the wool throw on the window seat across the room.

She let me sit there.

Then she said — and this is the line I wrote down too —

"You are not your father. You're sitting here. He didn't get this conversation. You are."

Near the end of the hour she mentioned, almost in passing, that there was one fermented postbiotic supplement she'd been recommending to her chronic-constipation patients for about a year.

A kombucha-derived gummy.

She wrote the name on a Post-it.

Jevawell.

A pre-fermented kombucha culture — the postbiotic matrix that delivers the organic acids my bacteria stopped making. Acetic. Lactic. Gluconic. The same molecules that activate the colon receptors my missing bacteria normally would have. Plus two probiotic strains with chronic-constipation trial data — L. plantarum and B. coagulans — to start rebuilding the populations that ferment the acids long-term. Inulin from dandelion root to feed what was left of my Bifido. Slippery elm to soothe the gut wall while the rebuild happens.

"I have no financial relationship with them," she said. "I just keep seeing my patients come back regular for the first time in a decade. You can search it."

She handed me the Post-it.

I put it in my wallet between the credit cards.

I drove home with the Post-it in my wallet and the microbiome chart on my phone.

I didn't go to the kitchen.

I went to my father's old desk in the spare room. The one my mother gave me when she sold the house.

Opened the bottom drawer.

Pulled out a manila folder of my father's last year of doctor's notes. I had kept them and never read them.

I read them at the desk at 10:30 PM with my husband asleep upstairs.

Twelve years of "increase MiraLAX dose."

Twelve years of "patient reports tightness, recommend stay the course."

Zero microbiome panels.

Zero discussion of bacteria.

Zero discussion of postbiotics.

I closed the folder. Sat with it on my lap.

He didn't know. His doctor didn't know.

I do know. I have the panel. I have the Post-it.

I pulled out my phone.

Typed in Jevawell.

Read the page. Kombucha culture, slippery elm bark, dandelion root, soluble fiber, the two probiotic strains. A prebiotic-probiotic-postbiotic stack. Sixty-day money-back guarantee.

Then I almost closed the tab.

I've fallen for Align. I've fallen for Milk of Magnesia. I've fallen for castor oil. I've fallen for twelve years of MiraLAX through my father's kitchen window.

What was a twenty-nine-dollar pouch of berry gummies going to do that thirty-dollar bottles of Align hadn't?

I almost closed the tab.

Then I pulled the Post-it out of my wallet.

Looked at Dr. Aurelia's handwriting.

I went back to the page and I ordered one pouch.

Then I changed the quantity to two.

One for now. One for when the first ran out.

The pouch arrived Thursday. Tracking said four days.

Cream-beige top panel. Dark green JEVAWELL wordmark with a little leaf in the A. Deep forest green body. Gold raspberry-and-leaves on the side.

I set it on the kitchen counter next to my father's old coffee scoop.

Looked at the two of them for a long minute.

Took one gummy.

Tasted berry.

Sat down at the kitchen table.

Week one — nothing.

Week two — nothing.

I almost emailed Dr. Aurelia to ask if I should keep going.

I didn't.

I kept taking the gummy.

Week three — Tuesday morning. I went, and the strain wasn't there. Twenty minutes, not ninety. The mass was softer. The movement was more complete.

I didn't tell anyone. I wasn't sure it counted.

Week five — three movements that week. Naturally. No MiraLAX since the parking-lot afternoon. No senna in the morning.

I told my husband over coffee on Saturday. He didn't say anything. He reached across the table and held my hand.

Week seven — regular daily. Soft. Easy. Twenty minutes a morning, not ninety.

The wrap dress fit again.

Week twelve — Dr. Aurelia repeated the panel.

Bifidobacterium up 54%.

Akkermansia up 41%.

Faecalibacterium up 67%.

Still not at "normal." But moving in the right direction for the first measurable time in my adult life.

She looked at the screen, then at me.

"We'll repeat this in six months. This is what a foundation looks like when you stop painting and start rebuilding."

It's been four and a half months now.

The orange Metamucil tubs are in the recycling.

The MiraLAX powder is still in the drawer, just in case. The scoop is dry. I haven't opened it since the parking lot.

The senna is on a high shelf I don't reach for.

The squatty potty got donated.

The wrap dress fits. I tucked a shirt in for the first time in three years last Tuesday and I wore it to work and didn't think about my stomach once.

The week of my father's anniversary, I had a hard stretch. Three days, the old tightness, the old dread loop. I took one more gummy at lunch instead of reaching for the laxative.

The body came back on its own by Wednesday.

The foundation is the foundation.

The weather still moves over it.

This past Sunday morning I sat at my parents' old kitchen table with a cup of coffee.

My mother makes the coffee in my father's old pot. The orange juice glass is still on the counter where he left it.

I drank the coffee and I went, by myself, without help, the first time in my adult life I have done that.

I came back to the kitchen and I sat down across from my mother.

I didn't tell her about the gummy.

I told her about Dr. Aurelia.

I told her about the panel.

I told her about the foundation and the painting.

She looked at me for a long time. Then she said, "I wish your father had heard that."

My father managed his output for twelve years.

He still died of the thing they were managing.

I fixed the cause.

In four months my gut bacteria are healthier than they've been in a decade.

If you're reading this — and your drawer looks like my drawer, and your doctor sounds like my father's doctor, and you have been managing the surface while the foundation rots underneath —

Stop repainting.

A fermented postbiotic. One gummy. A day. Sixty-day money-back guarantee — if it doesn't work, you send it back.

My father didn't get this conversation.

You are.

content.body:
On a Tuesday in April, a woman I'll call Marion was admitted to my floor with the most ordinary word in medicine sitting at the top of her chart: constipation. We'll sort it out.

The next Tuesday she died of it, in Room 9, and I was the nurse who charted "abdomen firm" the shift before it turned.

I've been a medical-surgical nurse for twenty-six years. I'm fifty-five. I am not a doctor. I'm not selling you my expertise, and I've never written anything like this in my life. But I have thought about Marion nearly every shift since April, and I've finally understood what I was standing next to that week. I need to tell you, because if you've read this far there's a decent chance I've been standing next to you too.

Let me tell you what those six days actually looked like, because the chart doesn't.

Marion was sixty-one. She came in for something else entirely — that part doesn't matter now — and somewhere in her intake was the line every nurse has typed a thousand times. Patient reports constipation. Hasn't gone in several days. Started on a bowel regimen.

You have to understand what "bowel regimen" means on a floor like mine. It's a ladder. Colace first. Then senna. Then a cap of MiraLAX. If none of that moves it, an enema. If the enema doesn't, magnesium citrate — the whole bottle. If that fails, someone puts on a glove. It is the most routine set of orders in the hospital. We run it on half the floor on any given night. Every rung of it manages the output. Not one rung of it asks why the body stopped doing the job on its own.

Marion climbed the whole ladder in four days.

Here's what nurses notice that the chart doesn't. It isn't the vital signs — hers were fine almost the whole way, which is exactly the problem. It's smaller than that. She stopped asking to get up to the bathroom. She got quiet in a way that isn't relief. When I pressed on her belly it was firm and it was silent, and a belly that's gone quiet is a belly that has stopped moving. I charted it. Abdomen firm, distended, hypoactive. I told the resident twice. It wasn't anyone's failure of caring — it was a Sunday, the floor was full, and constipation is the one thing every single person alive has had, so it's the last thing anyone takes seriously until it stops being constipation.

By Monday it was an obstruction. The wall gave out. The infection went into her blood, and she was gone by Tuesday morning — a week to the day after she'd walked in on her own two feet.

I've gone back over that week more times than I can tell you. Whether I pushed hard enough. Whether a louder nurse gets Marion to a scan on Saturday instead of Monday. I don't get to know that. What I do know is that I was standing three feet away with all my training, and the thing that killed her had been sitting under a word I'd stopped reading years ago.

The part I can't put down is the hallway.

Her daughter was out in the corridor outside Room 9 for most of that week, in the vinyl chairs we keep by the window. On the second day one of us asked her to bring in everything her mother took at home — we do that, it's called a medication reconciliation, you empty the whole cabinet into a bag and we sort it at the desk. She came back with a gallon freezer bag.

I sorted it myself at the nurses' station. I still see it.

MiraLAX. Metamucil. A bottle of magnesium and a second bottle of a different magnesium. Senna. Dulcolax. Milk of Magnesia. A dusty thing of castor oil. Align. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice. A jar of Triphala from some health store. Fiber gummies, two brands. There was a squatty potty at home, the daughter said — she just couldn't fit it in the bag.

Every one of them works on the stool. Softens it, bulks it, pulls water into it, forces the muscle to squeeze one time. Marion had a whole bag of things that manage the output, and she died of the one thing none of them were aimed at.

Three days after the notice went around the unit, I got home off a night shift and opened the drawer in my own bathroom to find my melatonin.

It was Marion's bag.

MiraLAX. The magnesium I take so I go every few days. The senna for when the magnesium doesn't. A box of Smooth Move I'm a little embarrassed about. Prune juice in the fridge downstairs.

I'm going to tell you the part I've never said out loud at work. I've had this myself for a decade. I go every four or five days, on a good stretch. Somewhere in my forties the urge just — left. I don't feel it come on the way I did at thirty. I go because I make myself go, or because the magnesium makes me. I manage it the way nurses manage their own bodies: quietly, on my own clock, telling myself I'll deal with it properly when the floor slows down. The floor never slows down.

I called her Marion in this letter to protect her. Standing at that drawer, I understood I could just as easily have called her me, a few years further along.

So I did the only thing I know how to do. I started asking questions, and I started reading.

The first person I asked was the GI attending — a woman I'll call Dr. Salinas — a few weeks later, on the floor. I asked her straight. How does a healthy sixty-one-year-old come in constipated and leave in a bag. Why does nobody catch this.

She didn't get defensive and she didn't blame anyone. She told me the honest thing.

"Because nothing looks for it," she said. "There's no scan for it. No blood test, nothing on a panel. Constipation is the most common complaint there is, so it reads as the least serious thing on the board. We get six minutes a patient. In six minutes you rule out the emergency and you send them home with the regimen. Nobody's trained to ask what's actually wrong underneath it — because underneath it doesn't show up on anything we can order."

Then she said the line I've kept. "Most of them are fine, Carol. They get the enema, they go home, you never think about them again. Marion is the one in a few hundred you don't forget."

She's right. In twenty-six years I've watched hundreds of admissions start exactly the way Marion's did. Most of them do go home. She's also right that some of them don't — and there's no test on the whole floor that tells you in advance which is which.

So on my nights off, I read. Not testimonials — the actual research, the way I'd read up on any diagnosis I didn't understand. And I found the thing nobody had told Marion, or me, in twenty-six years.

A few times a day, your colon is supposed to squeeze. One strong, sweeping contraction that moves everything down and out. That squeeze is what you feel as the urge. It's fired by a specific little band of cells in the wall of the colon. Pacemaker cells — the same basic idea as the ones that keep a heart on its beat.

In people like Marion, and like me, those cells have been wearing down for years. What wears them down is oxidation. Free radicals — produced inside your own gut in far too high a number — damaging the very cells that fire the contraction. And the reason they're overproduced isn't anything you did wrong. It's the ordinary modern stuff: years of processed food, stress, a couple of rounds of antibiotics. That thins out the good bacteria and leaves the lining raw, and a raw lining throws off these corrosive little molecules day and night. They don't switch off. The cells barely regrow, so the loss stacks up, year over year. The squeeze gets weaker. Then it comes less often. Then one day you notice the urge is just gone.

I read that at my kitchen table at one in the morning, and I put the paper down and went and got an apple.

I'd read that this is the same reaction that happens to a cut apple on the counter, and I wanted to see it for myself. I cut one in half and left it on a plate while I finished reading. Twenty minutes later the cut side had gone soft and brown. Nothing had touched it. That's free radicals, breaking the flesh down from the inside. Then I cut a fresh slice and squeezed lemon over it, and that one stayed white. That's an antioxidant — it steps in and neutralizes the free radicals before they can do the damage. It's the same chemistry that rusts a steel rail, running slow and quiet in the wall of the colon, on the cells that used to give you the urge without a second thought.

Here's the honest part — the part Dr. Salinas taught me to say. Nobody can put a scan on this. There was no test I could have run on Marion to catch it, and there's none I can run on myself. It is not a proven picture of anyone's colon. It is simply the best explanation there is for why a body that did everything right slowly stops going — and for why every test comes back normal the whole way down, the way Marion's did, the way mine always have.

And it finally explained the bag.

Fiber? Fiber is raw material your bacteria are supposed to ferment, but the same years that started this thinned those bacteria out, so the fiber just sits and turns to gas — which is why it made Marion more bloated, not less. You can't out-eat a contraction that isn't firing.

The stimulant laxatives — the senna, the Dulcolax — don't repair a thing. They lash the muscle into one forced squeeze. That's not the body going; that's the body being whipped into going. It works once, then it needs a bigger dose. Marion proved for years that her colon could be forced. She never once got the chance to find out whether it could work on its own.

The MiraLAX pulls water in so what's sitting there slides out. You go a little. Wet, full, still no urge — because the squeeze still isn't happening.

Even the prescription version — the one a doctor reaches for when the drawer stops working — forces the contraction from a different angle. Which only confirms the contraction is the missing piece. It doesn't stop what's damaging the cells, so as more of them wear down it works less and the dose climbs. Nobody on that whole ladder is aimed at the free radicals. That's the one rung that was never built.

Which left the obvious question. If the answer is an antioxidant, what antioxidant actually reaches the gut and does this.

The research kept coming back to one — kombucha, the fermented tea. Not as a trend. As a genuinely potent antioxidant that gets to the gut and calms the very activity that overproduces the free radicals in the first place.

So I did what any tired, skeptical nurse does. I bought the bottles. Three weeks of kombucha off the refrigerated shelf, and I felt nothing.

Then I read why. Heat is the one thing that destroys an antioxidant, and every shelf-stable bottle has been heated. Every "live" bottle is still fermenting in your fridge — making more alcohol and gas, not more of what you need. When they test these bottles, half don't even contain the acids printed on their own label, and one brand's active runs fifteen times stronger than another's. For the exact thing I was trying to get, the bottle is close to the worst form there is.

I hadn't failed at kombucha. The bottle had destroyed it before I ever drank it.

What I needed was the antioxidant kept intact, in a fixed amount, with the rest of the repair job handled too — the raw lining calmed, the good bacteria put back and fed. I built the list off the research. A concentrated kombucha extract for the free radicals. Slippery elm to settle the lining that's driving them. Two specific bacterial strains, each with its own trial in people with exactly this — one that helped people go more often, one that sped up how fast things moved through. And dandelion root to feed those strains so they actually take hold instead of washing straight out.

I was ready to assemble it out of five separate jars, the way I'd assembled everything else in that drawer. Then I found one that had put all of it in a single berry gummy — one a day. It's called Jevawell. A cream-topped pouch, deep forest green, a small gold raspberry on the front. Twenty-nine dollars. A sixty-day money-back guarantee, which — I'll come back to that.

I want to be honest about what the first week felt like, because I braced for the letdown I know by heart. The first week, nothing. I took the one gummy every morning with my coffee and waited to feel foolish.

What came first wasn't the thing I was watching for. I slept through the night — but that could be anything, I wasn't counting it. The bloat that always showed up by evening wasn't there by dinner — could be placebo, I wasn't counting that either. I had energy at the end of a shift where I usually didn't. My husband was the one who said it, at dinner, before I'd let myself claim any of it. "You didn't push your plate back tonight." I hadn't even noticed I'd stopped doing that.

Week two, on a Thursday, I went. On my own. No magnesium the night before, no bracing for it. I sat there afterward trying to remember the last time that had happened without a fight, and I couldn't.

I didn't tell anyone. I wasn't sure it counted.

Around week four the urge came back. The actual thing — my body telling me, instead of me telling my body. I hadn't felt that since my forties. And I hadn't touched the drawer in two weeks.

Here's the part that got me. Everything I'd ever tried had a quit date. The MiraLAX quit on me at six months. The magnesium quit and took my mood down with it every time. So I kept waiting, out of pure habit, for the week this one quit too. It came — a brutal stretch in the fall, a stomach bug, three days off the routine, the old dread setting back in. For the first time in a decade I didn't reach for the drawer. I kept taking the gummy, drank my water, and by the third day my body picked it back up on its own. That had never once happened before. Nothing quit.

I'm not the only one now. A night-shift nurse I'll call Rhonda caught me taking it in the break room, and I told her the whole thing. She'd been on MiraLAX longer than I had. A month in, she leaned on the counter at the start of a shift and said — her words — "I went this morning without thinking about it. First time in I don't know how long. I actually forgot to dread it." I wrote it down, because it's exactly right.

And eventually I told Dr. Salinas. Not to sell her anything — I just mentioned I'd stopped needing the magnesium, and why. She listened the way she listens. Then she said, "I don't have a study in front of me, and I'm not writing it on a chart. But whatever you're doing, keep doing it."

Something changed for me on the floor, too. I ask every patient one question now that I never used to ask. Not "are you regular" — nobody answers that one honestly. I ask, "When did you last actually go? No — really." You would not believe the answers. A week. Ten days. "I don't remember." Said calmly, the way Marion would have said it, by people who have no idea it's the first quiet rung of the same ladder.

I need to say one thing plainly, because I'm a nurse and I mean it. I am not telling anyone to stop anything their doctor prescribed. That is between you and them, and nothing here changes it. I'm telling you what I watched happen, what I read on my nights off, and what happened in my own body when I finally went after the cause instead of the output.

So let me say the thing I wish someone had said to Marion, in the six minutes nobody had.

If you go every four or five days, that's the contraction firing weak. If you've lost the urge — if you only go when you make yourself — that's the same contraction firing weaker.
